stories.title: Mixtapes and Intentionality
stories.description: Amit recounts making mixtapes for his girlfriend (now wife) when he was 19. He emphasizes the intentionality and effort involved in curating songs, calculating minutes per side, and recording them in real-time. It was an act of defining and sharing oneself, contrasting with the ease of sharing a Spotify playlist today.

stories.title: The CMIE Origin Story
stories.description: Ajay shares how his father, after getting sacked on April 13, 1976, immediately sat down and wrote inland letters to friends across India to start a new organization, CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy). This illustrates the power and necessity of physical correspondence in that era.

stories.title: Playboy in the Godrej Cupboard
stories.description: Amit found his father's locked stash of Playboy and Mayfair magazines (from 1967) in a Godrej cupboard. He reflects on how limited information about sex and the world was back then compared to the internet age, and how these magazines were a rare window into a different world.

stories.title: The Empty Diary
stories.description: Amit's father gave him 1986 diaries to write in. Amit started a novel 'Tales of St. John's' but only wrote a few chapters. He reflects on the scarcity of writing materials for many people and how having a diary was a privilege that shaped one's ability to practice writing.

stories.title: Visiting Cards: Creative Animal
stories.description: Amit shares his humorous visiting cards from his time at MTV, where his designation was 'Creative Animal' and later 'Manic Beast'. He contrasts this with the modern, sterile exchange of QR codes.

recommendations.comment: Amit reminisces about reading Enid Blyton's mystery series, which were a staple for children of his generation.
Ajay mentions Nehru's letters to his daughter, which became this book, as a prime example of the literary value of letter writing.
Ajay mentions that Tolkien's letters to his children evolved into The Hobbit.
Amit recommends this song by The Replacements from their album 'Let It Be', noting the poignancy of the line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?'.
Amit discusses Robin Dunbar's concept that humans can only maintain about 150 stable social relationships, and how physical address books were a manifestation of this.

core_ideas.description: The scarcity of the past (of time, information, objects) forced people to be more intentional, focused, and creative. Abundance (of content, communication) can lead to shallowness and a lack of focus.

core_ideas.item: We Shape Our Objects, They Shape Us
core_ideas.description: The physical nature of objects (e.g., a typewriter with no backspace, a limited-space diary) shapes how we think and create. Losing these objects changes our cognitive and emotional habits.

The shift from letters (asynchronous) to phone calls (synchronous) to instant messaging (quasi-synchronous) changes the nature of relationships. Asynchronous communication allowed for deeper, more composed thought.
Ajay argues that cash provides anonymity and freedom, whereas digital transactions create a panopticon where every move is traceable. He urges people to use cash to preserve this liberty.
In the past, people left on 'one-way journeys' with no guarantee of return or communication. Today, constant connectivity eliminates this profound human experience of separation and the 'unknown'.

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit's actual job titles on his visiting cards during his time at MTV.
Amit recounts a student from UP calling his mother from an STD booth and starting with a formal 'Pranam Mate' before switching to 'What the fuck happened?'.
Amit mentions a YouTube cooking video for Toddy Chicken as an example of the abundance of recipes today.
